body:
When reading through the requirements, requirement 16.5 stood out as different than the other requirements. It is the only one that references a code example. Specifically this section, "See [0x92-Appendix-C_CodeExamples.md](0x92-Appendix-C_CodeExamples.md) for an example of how you might approach this." 

Showing examples of how code can be written insecurely and showing exploits doesn't seem very helpful compared to positive examples - like a correctly written implementation. That said, creating code examples for any or all of the requirements seems like it would greatly expand the scope of the ASVS.

Any thoughts on going back to the old text for 16.5 and removing Appendix C?

comments.body:
I've completely renumber V16, and I think it now applies to 16.6.2. There is definitely a place for a long form ASVS, and I agree we should probably do what we do elsewhere, which is to reference one of the references below, rather than a seperate appendix.

@jmanico @danielcuthbert @tghosth - what do you think?

Yep @vanderaj, looks like you moved it 16.6.2 under the SSRF Protection Requirements.

Here is the current text for the requirement(16.6.2):

> Verify that untrusted data is not used within cross-domain resource sharing (CORS) to protect against arbitrary remote content. See 0x92-Appendix-C_CodeExamples.md for an example of how you might approach this.

I'm pretty sure this requirement isn't meant to avoid SSRF attacks. It is confusing in its current form, so I totally understand why it might have been miscategorized. Let me try to restate it.

"Verify that permissive CORS headers are not used as proof that data in the response from an HTTP request can be implicitly trusted and doesn't require input validation or output encoding."

The example in Appendix C shows an HTTP request from the browser, using XMLHttpRequest, to a user-provided URL. The response from that XMLHttpRequest is then inserted directly into an HTML entity without validation or output encoding.

I don't think this requirement(16.6.2) adds anything to the standard. The need to validate input is covered by 5.1.7, and output encoding by 5.2.2. 

Maybe there have been some real-world cases where developers thought that CORS was a trust signal and that response content can be trusted when CORS headers are present? Maybe response content was used in the way shown in Appendix C by some developer somewhere, but I can't imagine this is a widespread issue.
I agree with Ron to go back to the old text for 16.5 and removing Appendix C - and be done with it. Can you submit a pull request on this please?
@jmanico You merged my PR for this one. You can close it.

title: 16.5 and Appendix C: Code Examples
